newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh's appeals in bombing case may last years.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh's appeals in bombing case may last years.

text.p: Even if the jury decides that convicted Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh should be put to death, any execution would have to wait as his appeals could drag on for years, legal experts said on Tuesday.

They said McVeigh, found guilty on Monday on all 11 charges involving the April 19, 1995, Oklahoma City federal building bombing, would go to a U.S. appeals court and then to the U.S. Supreme Court no matter what punishment he receives.

"It will take a couple of years to wind its way through the appellate system," E. Lawrence Barcella, a former federal prosecutor, said, adding that any execution would be put off until McVeigh exhausts all of his appeals.

The Denver jury that convicted McVeigh, 29, a former Gulf War veteran, will reconvene on Wednesday to hear testimony on whether he should be sentenced to death by lethal injection or should get life in prison without the possibility of parole.
The experts agreed that prosecutors presented a strong, effective case against McVeigh and the conviction and sentence most likely would survive any legal challenge on appeal.

But they said McVeigh could challenge the 1994 federal law under which he was convicted, which expanded the number of crimes punishable by the death penalty, and also may challenge the trial judge's decision to limit evidence of the defence's alternative conspiracy theories for the bombing.
"He has some good arguments to make. Are they likely to be successful ones? No. There doesn't appear to be a lot of error that crept in during the trial," Barcella, a defence lawyer, said.

Barcella said state prosecutors in Oklahoma may bring their own charges against McVeigh, especially if he gets a life imprisonment sentence. State prosecutors may want to move quickly rather than waiting for McVeigh to finish his appeals.
"It is not uncommon in a highly visible case to have two prosecutions. Emotions in the state are too high not to do it. There are 160 other victims who need to have their rights vindicated," he said.

In Denver, McVeigh was found guilty of conspiracy, two bombing charges and eight counts of first-degree murder for eight federal law enforcement agents killed in the blast. The state charges would cover the others who died in the bombing.

George Washington University law professor Stephen Saltzburg, a former Justice Department official, estimated the appeals in the McVeigh case would take about 2-1/2 years. "If you get the death sentence, you want to delay this as long as you can, hoping to extend your life and (for) some favourable law decision," he said.

If McVeigh gets the death penalty, Saltzburg sees little need for a state prosecution. "They should let the judicial process work its way. Why do they need more than one death sentence? That ought to be enough."
Any conviction and sentence in Oklahoma could be appealed separately through state courts and then through the federal judiciary, up to the Supreme Court, Saltzburg said.

Sen. Don Nickles said a counter-terrorism law adopted by Congress and signed by President Bill Clinton last year would prevent lengthy appeals. "McVeigh won't be sitting on death row making endless appeals for the next 15-20 years" if he is sentenced to death, the Oklahoma Republican said on Monday.
According to the Justice Department, there are 12 defendants awaiting execution on federal death row. The last execution under a federal death penalty law was in 1963.
